extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientometricians, research evaluators, funders, and modelers interested in predicting long-term scholarly impact
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and evaluating statistical models (OLS and variants) that predict a publication's long-term citation impact by combining early citation counts, readership (Mendeley) metrics, and non-scientific publication features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early citation counts (L_IMPACT_t / L_IMPACT_t0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early citations—impact values measured at early time points after publication (e.g., IMPACT_t0 through IMPACT_t6). The coefficient for L_IMPACT_t steadily increases across iterations and is among the strongest predictors of long-term impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early citations, particularly within the first few years post-publication, remain among the strongest indicators of future impact. Use early-citation windows (0–2 years) as key predictors. Do NOT include all impact variables simultaneously in a predictive model because successive IMPACT_t variables are highly autocorrelated (e.g., corr between t0 and t1 = 0.77, t1–t2 = 0.96), which would cause severe multicollinearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mendeley readership (READ_t / L_READ_t)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mendeley readership measured at different time points (READ_t) used as a predictor; early readership correlates strongly with subsequent citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate early readership metrics (e.g., READ_t0) because they capture broader visibility and engagement and improve prediction especially in 0–2 year citation windows. Note that the predictive role of readership diminishes over longer time horizons (L_READ_t decreases from 0.278 at t0 to 0.070 at t6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal impact factor (L_IF)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hosting source's impact factor is included as a regressor (L_IF); it has a positive contribution early but its effect wanes and can become negative over longer time windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include journal impact factor as a predictor for early citation prediction; monitor its coefficient across time (positive at t0, decreasing and possibly negative by t6). It is particularly relevant in early iterations but loses explanatory power later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship characteristics (number of authors / L_AUTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics related to authorship, such as the number of authors (L_AUTH), included as predictors; L_AUTH shows a positive coefficient at t0 but turns negative in later iterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model authorship effects (co-authorship counts) because they influence initial visibility/citations; be aware the effect may reverse over time (becoming detrimental in later stages). Consider also accounting for field-dependent co-authorship norms via SC controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native English-speaking authorship (D_ENG)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummy variable indicating presence of a native English-speaking author; shows a small positive coefficient at t0 that turns negative by later time points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include language-composition indicators (D_ENG) to capture a possible early 'linguistic advantage.' Track temporal dynamics: initial positive effect may reverse over longer windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: International collaboration (D_FOREIGN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummy variable indicating when the address list contains more than one country (D_FOREIGN); correlated with D_ENG and associated with varying influence over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an international-collaboration indicator to capture visibility/impact advantages of multinational teams. Note correlation with D_ENG (reported corr = 0.60) and its diminishing coefficient over iterations (from 0.019 at t0 to 0.001 at t6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding presence (D_FUNDING)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummy variable capturing whether the publication reports funding (D_FUNDING); exhibits a negative trajectory over iterations (turns from positive to negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include funding indicators but be cautious: D_FUNDING may exert positive influence early and then decline or become negative in later prediction windows, so interpret effects as time-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access status (D_OPEN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummy variable for open access (D_OPEN); positive contributor to early impact but its effect lessens over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model open-access status as a predictor of early visibility. Expect diminishing long-term marginal effect; open access contributes to initial visibility but may not sustain citations over long horizons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of pages (L_PAGES / PAGES)
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the document (number of pages) included as L_PAGES/PAGES; shows positive influence early with decreasing coefficient over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include document length as a predictor—longer papers tend to receive more citations initially. Monitor declining influence across citation windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document type: Review vs Article (D_REW, D_ART)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummy variables indicating document type (review D_REW vs article D_ART); reviews initially have a strong positive coefficient which can turn negative over time; D_ART is inversely correlated and shows changing influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for document type because reviews and articles have different citation dynamics (e.g., D_REW correlated with number of references). Expect the initial positive advantage of reviews to decline in later windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references (L_REFER / REFER)
rubrics_metrics.description: The count of references in a publication used as a predictor; initially positive association with citations but may turn negative at later time points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reference-list size as a predictor (positively correlated with being a review and with pages). Watch for temporal reversal: positive early effects can become negative by t3–t6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject category (SC) fixed effects / SC dummies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a large set of dummy variables for subject categories (247 SC dummies) to control for disciplinary differences in citation practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always control for field/discipline via SC dummies to account for variability in citation patterns across fields. The study used 247 SC dummies (SC number 1 as baseline). Distribution of SC coefficients shifts with citation window (e.g., for t0 mean = -0.4; by t6 many SCs have positive coefficients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid including highly autocorrelated time series regressors simultaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact/readership values across successive years are highly autocorrelated (e.g., IMPACT t1–t2 corr = 0.96), so models that include all timepoint variables simultaneously are vulnerable to severe multicollinearity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construct predictive models that consider all impact variables at once. Selectively include time windows or transform variables to avoid multicollinearity. Check correlation matrices prior to model construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model specification: Full vs Reduced vs Completely Reduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare alternative model specifications: Full model (many predictors), Reduced model (fewer variables), and Completely Reduced model (IMPACT only + SC controls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more complex (Full) models to obtain higher explanatory power in early citation windows; simpler models (Reduced/Completely Reduced) converge in explanatory power for longer windows. Choose model complexity based on citation time window and parsimony considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model comparison metrics (Adjusted R² and ANOVA F-statistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Adjusted R² to assess explanatory power accounting for number of predictors; use ANOVA F-tests to evaluate whether additional predictors significantly improve explanatory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare models across time windows using Adjusted R² and ANOVA F-statistics. In this study the Full model had higher Adjusted R² in early iterations; all ANOVA comparisons yielded F values with p < 0.01 indicating Full model > Reduced models, though the F-statistic declines with longer citation windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checks on residuals (normality, outliers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-estimation analysis should examine residual distribution (histograms, kernel density, Q–Q plots) to assess normality and detect heavy tails or outliers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate normality of residuals visually and statistically; departures (especially in tails) can affect inference. If residuals show heavy tails or outliers, consider robust inference techniques (e.g., bootstrapping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bootstrap for robust inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply bootstrap procedures to estimate distributional properties of model coefficients when residuals deviate from normality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bootstrap resampling to obtain empirical Bias and Standard Error estimates for coefficients (the study used 500 iterations and reported minimal bias/SE). Bootstrapping provides more robust estimates when parametric assumptions are in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal framing of impact (short-term vs long-term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate short-term impact (within 6 years) and long-term impact (11 years after publication); predictors behave differently across these horizons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the citation time window explicitly when predicting long-term impact. Early windows (0–2 years) benefit most from non-citation predictors combined with early citations; long-term (e.g., 11 years) correlates more weakly with t0 citations and may require different modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider broader altmetrics and text-based features
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond Mendeley and citations, alternative metrics (social media, news, policy citations) and non-numeric text features (novelty, clarity, interdisciplinarity via NLP) may improve prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore incorporating altmetrics and machine-learning text features (NLP on abstracts, measures of novelty/interdisciplinarity) to capture non-numeric dimensions of influence not reflected in citations or readership alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability and contextual limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Results are based on Italian publications from 2010–2012; predictor importance may vary across countries, years, and disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test and validate models on datasets from other regions, time periods, and fields before generalizing. Be cautious about policy/funding decisions when models are trained on a narrow contextual sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle autocorrelation and temporal dynamics in predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and explicitly account for the strong temporal autocorrelation patterns in impact and readership measures (readership corr t0–t1 = 0.82; drops to 0.67 by t6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model temporal dependence carefully (e.g., lag structures, selective time-window predictors) and avoid naive inclusion of multiple consecutive timepoint predictors that induce multicollinearity. Use diagnostic correlation matrices to inform model design.
